chapter_theme: The ten of இல்லைப் பத்து names, line by line, the thing beyond which there is no greater of its kind: children as gain, knowing ஒப்புரவு as a fitting acquisition, attainable and unattainable desire as the best and worst desire, withholding as cruelty, lack of understanding as death, desire as poverty, renown as legacy, begging as disgrace and giving to askers as distinction.
structure_note: Line 51 carries the frame (ஆர்கலி யுலகத்து மக்கட்கெல்லாம்) shared by the ten. The lines fall in pairs: 53 and 54 are the same desire with and without fulfilment, and 59 and 60 are asking and giving to the asker; 57 (desire as poverty) leads into 59 (begging as disgrace).

51.reading: Of all gains a person can have, none is said to exceed the gain of children.
51.nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 51 is line 2 alone. The line is unconditional: it says children, not good or wise children, which is where it parts from Kural 61 and Innaa Narpathu 29.

items.claim: the getting of children is the greatest of gains

52.reading: No acquisition is said to be more fitting than knowing one's duty of ஒப்புரவு to the world.
52.nuance: The saying ranks the knowing (அறிதல்), not only the doing, and calls it a தகுவரவு, a fitting thing to come by: the duty is counted as a gain to the one who knows it, not a cost. வரவு as 'gain, what comes in' is our reading; it can also mean simply an arrival or attainment.

items.claim: knowing the duty of ஒப்புரவு is the most fitting thing to come by

53.reading: No desire is said to be better than a desire that can fittingly be fulfilled.
53.nuance: வாய்ப்புடை can mean 'having the chance of coming to pass' or 'fitting, proper'; on the first the line praises realistic desire, on the second lawful desire. 53 and 54 are a matched pair, the same word with and without its negative.

items.claim: a desire that can come to pass is the best of desires

54.reading: No desire is said to be worse than a desire that cannot come to pass.
54.nuance: The fault named is not the object of the desire but its futility: வாயா, 'that does not come about', makes wanting the unattainable the worst kind of wanting. If வாயா is read as 'unfitting', the line instead condemns improper desire.

items.claim: a desire that cannot be fulfilled is the worst of desires

55.reading: No cruelty is said to exceed hiding from others what one is able to give.
55.nuance: Refusal is classed as கொடுமை, cruelty, an active harm, not merely as a want of generosity; and the measure is இயைவது, what one can manage, so the poor man who cannot give is not touched by it.

items.claim: concealing what one could give is the greatest cruelty

56.reading: No death is said to be worse than being a person without understanding.
56.nuance: Bodily death is outranked by a living state: the senseless man is already dead in the sense that matters. உணர்வு may be taken narrowly as moral awareness or broadly as understanding.

items.claim: being without understanding is the worst death

57.reading: No poverty is said to be greater than desire.
57.nuance: Poverty is moved from what one has to what one wants: a man of means who still craves is, on this saying, the poorest of all.

58.reading: No legacy is said to be greater than renown.
58.nuance: எச்சம் is what a person leaves behind, and the word also means offspring; read against 51, the ten gives children the first place among gains in life and fame the first place among what outlasts it.

items.claim: renown is the greatest thing one leaves behind

59.reading: No disgrace is said to go beyond that of begging.

items.claim: asking of others is the deepest disgrace

60.reading: No distinction a person can reach is said to exceed that of giving to those who ask.
60.nuance: The ten closes on the counterpart of 59: the same act of asking is the asker's worst disgrace and the giver's highest distinction.

items.claim: giving to those who ask is the highest distinction one attains

links.note: Kural 61 knows no gain like children who come to know (அறிவறிந்த); the line names the getting of children the greatest gain with no condition.
links.teaches: The couplet's praise hangs on a single qualifier the line drops, so the pair shows the Kural deliberately narrowing a common saying that children are the greatest gain.
links.list_adds: Set first in a ten of superlatives that ranks fame as the greatest legacy (58) and giving as the greatest distinction (60), the line makes offspring one of several 'nothing greater' goods, so its supremacy is one claim among rival ones rather than the couplet's single ranking.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 29 counts begetting children without understanding (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) among painful things; the line calls the getting of children, unqualified, the greatest gain.
links.teaches: Read plainly, the two works give the same act opposite values, and only the qualifier about the child's understanding, which the Kural supplies, reconciles a supreme gain with a pain.

links.note: Kural 213 says nothing here or in the gods' world is as good as ஒப்புரவு; the line says nothing is a more fitting acquisition than knowing it.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks the duty itself above all goods; the line ranks the knowledge of the duty, so that merely learning what one owes the world already counts as the best thing one can gain.
links.list_adds: Placed in a ten of gains, losses and disgraces, the line turns ஒப்புரவு from a good done for others into an acquisition of the doer's own, set beside children and fame as things one gets.

links.note: 53 calls a desire that can come to pass the best desire; 54 calls a desire that cannot the worst.
links.teaches: Together the two lines judge desire by its outcome rather than its object, a scale on which the same wish is best or worst depending only on whether it can be fulfilled.

links.note: Thirikadugam 28 names the man who sits craving what he does not have (இல்லது காமுற்று இருப்பான்) as one who pounds husk; the line calls unattainable desire the worst desire.
links.teaches: Thirikadugam gives the image of the wasted labour and the line gives the verdict, so the pair says why futile wanting is worst: it spends effort with nothing to show.

links.note: Thirikadugam 45 says the man who without love hides what he can (இயைவ கரப்பான்) from those who ask falls into hell; the line uses the same words and calls the act the greatest cruelty.
links.teaches: The two works share the phrase for withholding what one can give, and between them name its moral kind (cruelty) and its fate (hell), so refusal is treated as a harm done to the asker, not just a lack of virtue.

links.note: Kural 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of begging and is destroyed at the thought of concealment; the line makes concealment the greatest cruelty.
links.teaches: The couplet weighs concealment by what it does to the asker's heart, the line by what it makes the concealer, and both rank it below begging itself, which 59 calls the worst disgrace.
links.list_adds: In a ten that also names begging the worst disgrace (59) and giving to askers the highest distinction (60), the line completes a three-way scoring of one exchange (asking, refusing, giving) that the couplet treats only from the asker's side.

links.note: 37 sets turning one's regard away from those one has taken from as no better than cruelty; 55 sets hiding what one can give as the greatest cruelty.
links.teaches: The book uses cruelty as the measure twice, once as a floor for ingratitude and once as a summit for refusal, so withholding from an asker ranks as worse than the ingratitude it is compared with.

links.note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting lives and anyone else is counted among the dead; the line calls being without understanding the worst death.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the living death a matter of not knowing ஒப்புரவு; the line widens it to any lack of understanding and ranks it below bodily death, while 52 in the same ten keeps the couplet's other half, knowing ஒப்புரவு as the best gain.
links.list_adds: The ten splits the couplet's antithesis across two separate lines (52 and 56), so knowing one's duty and lacking understanding become a highest gain and a worst death in a series of superlatives.

links.note: Kural 363 calls not wanting the finest wealth here and hereafter; the line calls wanting the greatest poverty.
links.teaches: The couplet makes desirelessness a wealth and the line makes desire a poverty, so together they move both wealth and poverty out of possessions and into the state of wanting.
links.list_adds: Placed two lines before begging is named the worst disgrace (59), the line sets desire as the poverty that leads to asking, a causal sequence the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Naladiyar 306 says a mind racked by desire (காதல் கவற்றும் மனம்) sends a man to beg of strangers when he could end his want by asking of himself; the line calls desire the greatest poverty.
links.teaches: The quatrain shows the mechanism the line only names: it is desire, not lack, that drives a man to beg, so the poverty that matters is the one inside.
links.list_adds: The line states the root in four words, as one of ten superlatives, where the quatrain needs a scene and a remedy; set beside 59, the ten's list makes desire and begging the worst poverty and the worst disgrace.

links.note: Kural 238 calls it a disgrace not to obtain the legacy called renown (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்); the line, using the same two words, calls renown the greatest legacy.
links.teaches: The couplet makes renown the minimum below which a life is disgraced; the line makes it the maximum above which there is no legacy, so the pair fixes fame as both the floor and the ceiling of what one leaves.
links.list_adds: In a ten that opens with children as the greatest gain (51), the line separates the legacy of fame from the gain of offspring, two senses that the couplet's எச்சம் leaves folded together.

links.note: 51 names the getting of children the greatest gain; 58 names renown the greatest எச்சம், a word that also means offspring.
links.teaches: Within one ten the two superlatives divide the field: children are the greatest gain in life, but what survives a person is ranked as fame, not progeny.

links.note: 59 makes begging the deepest disgrace; 60 makes giving to those who beg the highest distinction.
links.teaches: The ten scores one exchange twice, from both sides, so the asker's lowest point is the giver's highest, the same thing seen as shame and as honour.

links.note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even for water for a cow; the line says no disgrace goes beyond begging.
links.teaches: The couplet tests the claim at its hardest case, a worthy cause and a tiny request, while the line states it bare, so the pair shows the superlative holds without exception for need or motive.
links.list_adds: Coupled with 60, the line's list sets the asker's disgrace beside the giver's distinction, so begging is judged inside an exchange rather than alone as the couplet judges it.

links.note: Purananuru 204 says giving at 'take' is high and refusing a gift is higher still (கொள்ளேன் என்றல் அதனினும் உயர்ந்தன்று); the line says no distinction exceeds giving to those who ask. The tension holds on the plain reading of the line's 'nothing greater'.
links.teaches: The bard's poem ranks the proud refusal of a gift above the gift, where the ethics line puts the giver at the summit, showing the puram ethic of honour placing the poet's self-respect above the patron's generosity.

links.note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown are the only profit of life; the line ranks giving to askers as the highest distinction.
links.teaches: The couplet treats giving as a means to renown, the only profit; the line narrows the gift to one made to those who ask and makes its distinction an end, so the asker's presence is what makes the gift supreme.
links.list_adds: The ten sets giving to askers directly after begging as the worst disgrace (59), so the giver's distinction is ranked against the asker's shame, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

source_issues: 51: the comparison site's text lacks line 2 (மக்கட் பேற்றின் பெறும்பே(று) இல்லை), the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line. பெறும்பே(று) carries an editorial bracket for the elided final vowel.
58, 60: word division is irregular in print (எச்ச மில்லை for எச்சம் இல்லை; சிறப்பில்லை run together).
59: ஊஉங்கு is written with the lengthening vowel (அளபெடை) for ஊங்கு.
